title: Chapter 3: Your First Python AI App
content:
Chapter 3: Your First Python AI App

From a Reusable Client to a Command-Line Assistant

The code explainer in Chapter 1 introduced a model call, and Chapter 2 moved that call into a reusable LLM client. You can now build an application around it: a command-line assistant that accepts a request, chooses a prompt, displays the answer and waits for the next request.

The assistant will offer four modes: /ask, /explain, /summarize and /tasks. Each mode uses the same client, but gives the model different instructions. Keeping those instructions separate from command handling will let you change an explanation prompt without disturbing the terminal interface.

What You Will Learn

This chapter follows a request through the application, from typed input to displayed response. You will learn to:

  • Divide a small Python app into files with clear responsibilities.
  • Parse commands, check their content and route them to an assistant mode.
  • Build reusable prompts and request answers with consistent sections.
  • Connect those prompts to the LLM client from Chapter 2.
  • Test prompt builders, command parsing and routing without live API calls.
  • Provide a terminal interface with help, error messages and a way to exit.

Organising the Project

As you add modes, it becomes harder to follow a program that mixes prompt text, API configuration and user interaction in one place. A small change can then affect code you did not intend to touch. The project separates these responsibilities so you can find, test and revise each part:

  • llm_client.py handles model access.
  • prompts.py stores prompt templates.
  • commands.py parses user input.
  • assistant.py connects commands to prompts and the client.
  • app.py handles terminal input and output.
  • The tests check the behaviour of these parts.
  • README.md explains how to set up and use the project.

This division will also be useful when later chapters add document retrieval, tools, memory and a web interface. You will be able to see which part of the application each new feature belongs to.

3.1 What Makes Something an AI App?

The model generates text, but the surrounding Python code decides what the user can do with it. In this assistant, that code manages the interface, validates input, constructs prompts, calls the model, displays responses and handles errors. A loop allows repeated interaction until the user exits.

The terminal is enough for this project. Working without a web interface keeps your attention on the request flow and makes it easier to inspect a problem when a command behaves unexpectedly.

3.2 The Input/Output Flow

For each request, the app follows these steps:

  1. Read the user's command.
  2. Separate the command from its content.
  3. Select the corresponding prompt template.
  4. Send the completed prompt to the LLM client.
  5. Print the response and wait for another command.

Suppose the user enters:

/explain Python dictionaries

The parser separates it into two parts:

Command parser:
command = /explain
content = Python dictionaries

The prompt builder uses the content to complete an instruction beginning Explain this Python concept for a beginner.... The client sends that prompt to the model, and the app prints the returned explanation. Later projects will add steps to this flow, but command handling and model access will remain distinct responsibilities.

3.3 Why Prompt Templates Matter

A prompt template keeps the instruction fixed while allowing the subject to change. For example:

Explain the following Python concept for a beginner:

{concept}

A builder inserts the requested concept into this template. Because the instruction lives in prompts.py, you can revise it in one place and test that it includes both the concept and the required directions. You can also inspect the resulting string before making an API call, which helps separate a prompt-construction problem from a model-response problem.

3.4 Structured Responses

An instruction such as Explain this. leaves the answer's organisation open. If a reader needs a definition, an example and a practice step, ask for those parts explicitly:

Return your answer with these sections:
1. Short answer
2. Explanation
3. Example
4. Common mistake
5. Next step

These headings give the reader a familiar way to navigate answers. They also give you something concrete to check during evaluation: Chapter 11 will use required sections as one check on an output. The headings are a formatting request, however; their presence alone does not establish that the answer is correct.

3.5 Project: Command-Line AI Assistant

Commands and Modes

The assistant supports these commands:

/help
/ask
/explain
/summarize
/tasks
/exit

Use /help to see the options and /exit to quit. The other commands take content after the command name:

/ask What is RAG?
/explain Python list comprehensions
/summarize Python is a popular language because...
/tasks Build a PDF chatbot portfolio project

Who Can Use It

A Python learner can use the explanation mode while studying; a student or developer can summarise notes or draft a task plan. For a freelancer or someone beginning AI development, the project provides a small application whose routing, prompts and tests are easy to inspect and adapt.

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_03_cli_ai_app
cd chapter_03_cli_ai_app

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate the environment using the command for your operating system. On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

Create requirements.txt with these versions, used for this edition’s offline tests:

openai==3.13.0
python-dotenv==1.2.3
pytest==9.1.1
httpx2==2.12.0

Install the dependencies in the active virtual environment:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini
OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy the example to .env. On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit .env and replace the placeholder with your API key. Keep that file private; the example file can be shared because it contains a placeholder rather than a credential.

3.8 File: llm_client.py

"""Reusable model client; importing or constructing it makes no API request."""
import math
import os
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Protocol

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI, OpenAIError


def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:
    """Read a finite float, returning the default for invalid settings."""
    try:
        value = float(os.getenv(name, str(default)))
    except ValueError:
        return default
    return value if math.isfinite(value) else default


@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
    """Configuration for the source chapter's gpt-4.1-mini model."""
    model: str = field(default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini"))
    temperature: float = field(default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2))


class LLMProvider(Protocol):
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        """Return model-generated text."""
        ...


class LLMClient:
    """Use an injected SDK client in tests; initialise the real SDK on demand."""
    def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None, client: Any = None):
        # Read only the project's explicit .env, rather than searching parent folders.
        load_dotenv(".env", override=False)
        self.config = config or LLMConfig()
        self.client = client

    def build_input(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        """Validate both messages and return the original combined-text representation."""
        if not system.strip():
            raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
        if not user.strip():
            raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")
        return f"System instruction:\n{system.strip()}\n\nUser request:\n{user.strip()}"

    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        self.build_input(system, user)
        if not self.config.model.strip():
            raise ValueError("OPENAI_MODEL cannot be empty.")
        if not math.isfinite(self.config.temperature) or not 0 <= self.config.temperature <= 2:
            raise ValueError("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE must be between 0 and 2.")
        if self.client is None:
            api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", "").strip()
            if not api_key or api_key == "replace_with_your_api_key":
                raise ValueError("OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file.")
            self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key)
        try:
            response = self.client.responses.create(
                model=self.config.model,
                instructions=system.strip(),
                input=user.strip(),
                temperature=self.config.temperature,
            )
        except OpenAIError as error:
            raise RuntimeError("Model request failed. Check your network and API account, then retry.") from error
        output = response.output_text
        if not isinstance(output, str) or not output.strip():
            raise RuntimeError("The model returned no text. Please retry or inspect the provider response.")
        return output


class MockLLMClient:
    """Explicit local test double; its fixed answer is not a real model result."""
    def __init__(self, response_text: str = "Mock response"):
        self.response_text = response_text
        self.calls: list[dict[str, str]] = []

    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        if not system.strip():
            raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
        if not user.strip():
            raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")
        self.calls.append({"system": system, "user": user})
        return self.response_text

3.9 File: prompts.py

"""Prompt templates for the command-line AI assistant."""

GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a helpful AI assistant for beginner-to-intermediate Python learners.
Be clear, practical, and honest. Avoid unnecessary jargon.
Do not invent facts. If you are unsure, say what is uncertain.
"""
PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a friendly Python tutor.
Explain Python concepts clearly for beginner-to-intermediate learners.
Use simple examples. Mention common mistakes when helpful.
Do not claim that you executed code unless execution actually happened.
"""
SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a careful summarization assistant.
Summarize only the text provided by the user.
Do not add facts that are not present in the text.
Keep the summary clear and useful.
"""
TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a practical task planning assistant.
Turn goals into clear, realistic task lists. Do not overpromise.
Include human review when the task involves important decisions.
"""


def build_general_prompt(question: str) -> str:
    return f"""
Answer the following question clearly and practically:

{question}

Return:
1. Short answer
2. Explanation
3. Example or practical note
4. Next step
"""


def build_python_explanation_prompt(concept: str) -> str:
    return f"""
Explain this Python concept for a beginner-to-intermediate learner:

{concept}

Return:
1. Simple definition
2. Why it matters
3. Short Python example
4. Common beginner mistake
5. Practice idea
"""


def build_summary_prompt(text: str) -> str:
    return f"""
Summarize the following text:

{text}

Return:
1. One-sentence summary
2. Key points
3. Important details
4. Suggested title

Rules:
- Use only the provided text.
- Do not invent information.
"""


def build_task_plan_prompt(goal: str) -> str:
    return f"""
Create a practical task plan for this goal:

{goal}

Return:
Goal:
A short restatement of the goal.

Tasks:
A numbered list of clear steps.

Risks:
Possible risks or unclear areas.

Next Action:
The first action the user should take.

Rules:
- Keep the plan realistic.
- Do not invent deadlines, prices, or guarantees.
"""

3.10 File: commands.py

"""Parse the source chapter's six commands; ordinary text becomes /ask."""
from dataclasses import dataclass

SUPPORTED_COMMANDS = {"/help", "/ask", "/explain", "/summarize", "/tasks", "/exit"}


@dataclass
class ParsedCommand:
    command: str
    content: str


def parse_command(user_input: str) -> ParsedCommand:
    cleaned = user_input.strip()
    if not cleaned:
        return ParsedCommand(command="", content="")
    if not cleaned.startswith("/"):
        return ParsedCommand(command="/ask", content=cleaned)
    parts = cleaned.split(maxsplit=1)
    command = parts[0].lower()
    content = parts[1].strip() if len(parts) > 1 else ""
    return ParsedCommand(command=command, content=content)


def is_supported_command(command: str) -> bool:
    return command in SUPPORTED_COMMANDS


def help_text() -> str:
    return """
Available commands:

/help
    Show this help message.
/ask [question]
    Ask a general AI question. Example: /ask What is RAG?
/explain [Python concept]
    Explain a Python concept. Example: /explain list comprehensions
/summarize [text]
    Summarize provided text. Example: /summarize Python is popular because...
/tasks [goal]
    Create a task plan. Example: /tasks Build a PDF chatbot
/exit
    Quit the assistant.

Tip: You can also type a normal question without a command.
It will be treated as /ask.
""".strip()

3.11 File: assistant.py

"""Connect commands and prompts to the injected or real model client."""
from commands import parse_command, is_supported_command, help_text
from llm_client import LLMClient, LLMProvider
from prompts import (
    GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    build_general_prompt,
    build_python_explanation_prompt,
    build_summary_prompt,
    build_task_plan_prompt,
)


def require_content(command: str, content: str) -> str | None:
    if content.strip():
        return None
    examples = {
        "/ask": "Example: /ask What is RAG?",
        "/explain": "Example: /explain Python dictionaries",
        "/summarize": "Example: /summarize Paste text here.",
        "/tasks": "Example: /tasks Build a PDF chatbot",
    }
    example = examples.get(command, "Please provide content.")
    return f"Missing content for {command}.\n{example}"


def handle_command(user_input: str, client: LLMProvider | None = None) -> str:
    parsed = parse_command(user_input)
    if not parsed.command:
        return "Please enter a command or question."
    if parsed.command == "/exit":
        return "EXIT"
    if parsed.command == "/help":
        return help_text()
    if not is_supported_command(parsed.command):
        return f"Unknown command: {parsed.command}\nType /help to see available commands."
    missing_message = require_content(parsed.command, parsed.content)
    if missing_message:
        return missing_message
    llm = client if client is not None else LLMClient()
    if parsed.command == "/ask":
        return llm.complete(system=GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_general_prompt(parsed.content))
    if parsed.command == "/explain":
        return llm.complete(system=PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_python_explanation_prompt(parsed.content))
    if parsed.command == "/summarize":
        return llm.complete(system=SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_summary_prompt(parsed.content))
    if parsed.command == "/tasks":
        return llm.complete(system=TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_task_plan_prompt(parsed.content))
    return "Command was recognized but not handled."

3.12 File: app.py

"""Chapter 3: Command-Line AI Assistant."""
from assistant import handle_command
from llm_client import LLMProvider


def print_welcome() -> None:
    print("\nCommand-Line AI Assistant")
    print("=" * 45)
    print("Type /help to see commands.")
    print("Type /exit to quit.")
    print("=" * 45)


def main(client: LLMProvider | None = None) -> None:
    """Run the CLI. An optional injected client supports offline integration tests."""
    print_welcome()
    while True:
        try:
            user_input = input("\nYou: ").strip()
            response = handle_command(user_input, client=client)
            if response == "EXIT":
                print("\nAssistant: Goodbye.")
                break
            print("\nAssistant:")
            print(response)
        except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
            print("\n\nAssistant: Goodbye.")
            break
        except Exception as error:
            print("\nAssistant:")
            print(f"Something went wrong: {error}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from prompts import (
    build_general_prompt, build_python_explanation_prompt,
    build_summary_prompt, build_task_plan_prompt,

def test_build_general_prompt_contains_question():
    prompt = build_general_prompt("What is RAG?")
    assert "What is RAG?" in prompt

def test_build_python_explanation_prompt_contains_concept():

    assert "Simple definition" in prompt
    assert "Short Python example" in prompt


def test_build_summary_prompt_contains_text():
    prompt = build_summary_prompt("Python is useful for automation.")
    assert "Python is useful for automation." in prompt
    assert "One-sentence summary" in prompt
    assert "Do not invent information" in prompt


def test_build_task_plan_prompt_contains_goal():
    prompt = build_task_plan_prompt("Build a PDF chatbot")
    assert "Build a PDF chatbot" in prompt
    assert "Goal:" in prompt
    assert "Tasks:" in prompt
    assert "Risks:" in prompt

from commands import parse_command, is_supported_command, help_text


def test_parse_command_with_slash_command():

    assert parsed.command == "/ask"
    assert parsed.content == "What is Python?"

    assert "/explain" in text

    assert "Python dictionaries" in mock.calls[0]["user"]

    mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock summary")
    assert handle_command("/summarize Python is useful for AI.", client=mock) == "Mock summary"
    assert len(mock.calls) == 1


def test_handle_tasks_uses_mock_client():
    mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock task plan")
    assert handle_command("/tasks Build a chatbot", client=mock) == "Mock task plan"
    assert len(mock.calls) == 1

3.16 File: README.md

# Command-Line AI Assistant

Chapter 3 of *Agentic AI With Python* by Ronik Basak. This independent project preserves the original command parser, four prompt modes, model-client interface and twenty source tests. Code reconstruction restores Python indentation, multiline strings and module entrypoints.

## Setup

Use Python 3.11 or later. Work inside this project folder so imports and `.env` lookup refer to this project.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Windows PowerShell activation: `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`.

Tests, `/help`, `/exit` and the offline example do not need a key:

```bash
python -m pytest
python offline_example.py
python app.py
```

To generate a real answer, copy `.env.example` to `.env` (`cp .env.example .env`, or `Copy-Item .env.example .env` in PowerShell) and supply your own OpenAI API key. Keep `.env` private. The source model default remains `gpt-4.1-mini`. A model request uses your provider account and can incur charges. No provider-network requests were used to validate this companion.

## Commands

```text
/help
/ask What is RAG?
/explain Python list comprehensions
/summarize Python is popular because it is readable and has many libraries.
/tasks Build a PDF chatbot portfolio project
/exit
```

Normal text becomes `/ask`. Commands are case-insensitive, while their content keeps its original case. Missing content and unknown commands return guidance without a model call. Ctrl+C and end-of-input quit normally.

## Repairs and validation

- All original public functions and six commands remain available.
- `LLMClient.complete(system, user)` initialises the real SDK only when needed; an injected client allows offline tests. The provider request uses distinct `instructions` and `input` fields. `build_input()` remains available as the original validated combined-text representation.
- Invalid/non-finite numeric environment values fall back to the documented default; invalid configured temperature, missing keys and blank provider output produce clear errors.
- SDK errors are surfaced as a concise model-request failure. These messages do not include raw provider response bodies.
- The original twenty tests pass. Ten added regressions cover missing-command behavior, parser case, lazy credentials, invalid configuration, blank provider output, real SDK serialization through a local HTTP mock, provider failure and executable CLI sessions.
- `test-output.txt` and `test-results.xml` contain the actual local run: **30 passed**. The SDK integration fixture uses the real installed OpenAI client with `httpx2.MockTransport`; its answers are fixed test data, not live model output.

## Limits

This is a teaching application. Prompt headings request a format but do not validate answer correctness. Live credentials, provider-network availability, model quality, latency and billing were not tested. It reads one terminal line per request; multiline entry and saved conversation history remain exercises. Keep each chapter's tests in its own project directory because module names repeat across projects.

3.17 How the Code Works

Follow a request through the five layers below. Each excerpt shows part of the application and assumes the surrounding imports and values from the full files. Run python offline_example.py for a complete local demonstration with an explicitly labelled mock response.

Layer 1: User Interface

app.py prints the welcome message, reads input and displays the response returned by handle_command():

response = handle_command(user_input)

The interface does not need to select a prompt or know which model is configured. It passes the request on and deals with what comes back.

Layer 2: Command Parsing

commands.py separates a command from the text that follows it. For example, /explain Python dictionaries becomes:

ParsedCommand(
    command="/explain",
    content="Python dictionaries",
)

A question without a slash command defaults to /ask. The input What is RAG? therefore becomes:

ParsedCommand(
    command="/ask",
    content="What is RAG?",
)

This default lets someone ask a question immediately, while explicit commands remain available for other tasks.

Layer 3: Prompt Templates

prompts.py turns the parsed content into instructions. For example:

build_python_explanation_prompt("Python dictionaries")

This call returns a string asking for an explanation with defined sections. Constructing that string does not require a live model call, so the prompt builder can be tested on its own.

Layer 4: Assistant Logic

assistant.py selects the prompt pair for each mode. For /summarize, it uses:

system = SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT
user = build_summary_prompt("Python is useful for automation.")

For /tasks, it uses:

system = TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT
user = build_task_plan_prompt("Build a PDF chatbot")

This is also where the app handles unsupported commands and missing content before creating a client or sending a request.

Layer 5: LLM Client

llm_client.py contains the provider-specific call. The assistant asks it for text through a common interface:

response = llm.complete(system=system, user=user)

The mock client offers the same interface but returns a fixed response and records the call. The real client is created only when a model request is needed, so imports, help, exit and local tests do not need a key. Its provider request sends the system instruction and user text in separate fields. Those changes make local tests practical without claiming that they validate live answers.

3.18 Sample User Session

The following example illustrates the interaction and the requested answer structure. It is sample output, not a captured execution; your model's wording may differ.

Command-Line AI Assistant
=============================================
Type /help to see commands.
Type /exit to quit.
=============================================

You: /explain Python dictionaries

Assistant:
1. Simple definition

A Python dictionary is a collection that stores data as key-value pairs.

2. Why it matters

Dictionaries are useful when you want to look up information by name or label.

3. Short Python example

person = {"name": "Asha", "age": 25}
print(person["name"])

4. Common beginner mistake

A common mistake is trying to access a key that does not exist.

5. Practice idea

Create a dictionary for a book with title, author, and year.

If you include results in your own documentation, run the application and capture what it actually returns.

3.19 Testing the Project

Run the tests from the project folder:

python -m pytest

The reconstructed companion passed its local test suite with this summary:

30 passed

The companion contains the twenty original tests and ten regression checks. Read test-output.txt and test-results.xml for the captured run. Your count will change if you add or remove tests.

The tests cover prompt builders, command parsing, help text, missing-content checks, routing and mock-client calls. Added checks exercise the terminal loop, end-of-input, lazy credentials, invalid settings, provider errors and the real OpenAI SDK with a local HTTP response fixture. No live model request is made; model quality still needs a separate live check.

3.20 Live API Testing

With your API key in .env, start the app:

python app.py

Try each command, including help and exit:

/help
/ask What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
/explain Python list comprehensions
/summarize Python is widely used for automation, data analysis, AI, and web development because it is readable and has a large ecosystem.
/tasks Build a Python AI portfolio project
/exit

Read the answers as a learner would. Check whether the explanation is understandable, the requested sections are present and the examples fit the question. Look for unsupported certainty as well as obvious errors. Live model requests use your API account, so keep these checks deliberate and review the results before expanding them.

3.21 How This Structure Supports Later Projects

The app now separates commands, prompts, assistant logic, model access, tests and documentation. Its main path is a selected mode followed by a prompt, a model call and an answer with requested sections. You can extend that path while retaining the surrounding organisation.

Chapter 4 adds document question-answering, Chapter 6 introduces tool use, and Chapter 8 develops workflow automation. Chapter 12 brings these ideas into a deployed web app. The terminal project gives you a smaller setting in which to understand their shared structure first.

3.22 Structured Output Habits

The /tasks prompt asks for these headings:

Goal:
Tasks:
Risks:
Next Action:

They separate the proposed work from its uncertainties and first action. When an answer is difficult to use, you can inspect which section is missing or unclear instead of judging the response only by its overall tone.

Later, these headings can support formatting checks, evaluation and automation. A text prompt still only requests the structure: your code must check the returned text before relying on it. A well-formatted plan can also contain poor advice, so content review remains necessary.

3.23 Uses for the Assistant

Learning

While studying Python, request an explanation of a concept you have just encountered:

/explain Python decorators

Summarisation

Condense notes or a short passage using the summarisation mode:

/summarize [paste text]

Planning

Ask for a first draft of the steps involved in a goal, then revise them for your circumstances:

/tasks Prepare for a Python interview

Productivity

Use the terminal to ask a question while you are working:

/ask What is semantic search?

Development

Use the files and tests as a starting point for another assistant. Adding a mode gives you practice in changing a parser, writing a prompt and checking the routing without also having to build a web interface.

3.24 Portfolio and Service Possibilities

Present the project as Command-Line AI Assistant. A description should tell a reviewer what it does and how it is organised:

A Python command-line assistant for Q&A, Python explanations, summarisation and task planning. It separates command parsing, prompt templates and model access, with a mock client for testing application logic without API calls.

In a demonstration, trace one command from input to response. Show how the configuration is loaded, where the prompt lives and what the tests check. This gives a reviewer evidence of your approach to app structure, reuse and user interaction.

Possible extensions include an internal team assistant, a developer helper, a study assistant or a specialised command-line utility. Treat these as starting points for a service discussion. A client's requirements, data handling and expected behaviour still need to be established before you can offer a finished product.

3.25 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Putting Everything in app.py

When terminal interaction, prompts and API calls share one file, it becomes harder to test a part independently. Keep those responsibilities in commands.py, prompts.py, assistant.py and llm_client.py, leaving app.py to manage the interface.

Mistake 2: Mixing Prompt Text with the App Loop

Put prompt templates in prompts.py, where you can inspect and edit them without following the terminal loop. Tests can then check the resulting strings directly.

Mistake 3: Calling the API in Every Test

Use the mock client when checking routing and prompt construction. Reserve live calls for integration testing and model-response validation, where the provider's actual behaviour is part of what you need to assess.

Mistake 4: Omitting Command Help

Include /help with examples so users can discover the commands while the app is running.

Mistake 5: Omitting an Exit Command

Provide /exit and make it visible in the welcome message. Quitting should be a normal part of the interaction.

Mistake 6: Leaving the Answer Format Unspecified

Ask for sections that suit the task, then check whether the model supplies them. A summary and a task plan need different structures.

Mistake 7: Ignoring Empty Input

Check for an empty command or missing content before contacting the model. Return an example of the expected input so the user knows how to continue.

3.26 Practices to Keep as the App Grows

Keep each file focused on its role, and add a prompt and routing test whenever you add a mode. Validate input before a model call, keep /help up to date and retain a clear exit path.

Use the reusable client for model access and the mock client for local tests. Keep credentials in the private .env file, and update the README when setup or usage changes. These habits help another person run the project and help you return to it after time away.

3.27 Mini Challenges

Challenge 1: Add a /rewrite Command

Add /rewrite [text] to revise a passage for clarity and a professional tone. Have the prompt request these sections:

Improved version:
What changed:

Challenge 2: Add a /quiz Command

Add /quiz [topic] and ask for five quiz questions suitable for a beginner studying that topic.

Challenge 3: Add a /save Feature

Save the last assistant response to last_response.md so the user can keep it after the session ends.

Challenge 4: Add Conversation History

Store the last three user messages during the current session. Keep this history in memory for now, without saving it permanently.

Challenge 5: Add Response Length Options

Support the following forms and adjust the prompt to match the requested level of detail:

/ask short What is RAG?
/ask detailed What is RAG?

3.28 Chapter Summary

The command-line assistant brings four modes together: general Q&A, Python explanation, summarisation and task planning. Its files separate the interface, command parsing, prompt construction, routing and model client, while tests check the application logic through a mock client.

In Chapter 4, you will add RAG, or Retrieval-Augmented Generation. That project will supply the model with text retrieved from a document so it can attempt to answer questions about that material.

Key Takeaways

  • Command parsing gives each request a mode and content that the assistant can handle separately.
  • Prompt templates centralise instructions; requested headings make responses easier to inspect.
  • A reusable client keeps provider-specific calls out of the interface and routing logic.
  • Mock tests check application behaviour without live API calls. They do not establish the quality of a model's answers.
  • The same separation of responsibilities will support later work on RAG, tools, memory, workflows and deployment.
